title: Excitonic Magnetism in Ruthenium Pyrochlores
authors: Swetlana Swarup, Yang Yang, Natalia B. Perkins
abstract: Strong spin-orbit coupling in $d^4$ systems is expected to stabilize a nonmagnetic $J=0$ singlet ground state, yet many ruthenium pyrochlores exhibit robust long-range magnetic order. Motivated by this apparent contradiction, we develop a microscopic theory of Van Vleck excitonic magnetism on the pyrochlore lattice. Starting from a multi-orbital Hubbard model with spin-orbit coupling, we derive the effective superexchange interactions within the low-energy singlet--triplet manifold of Ru$^{4+}$ ions. We analyze the resulting excitonic Hamiltonian using both the spectrum of triplon excitations and a variational treatment of the condensed phase. We identify the instability of the nonmagnetic singlet state toward triplon condensation and determine the resulting magnetic phase diagram as a function of the microscopic hopping parameters. The phase diagram reproduces the magnetic orders known from conventional pyrochlore models while also predicting an additional magnetic phase unique to the singlet--triplet description. Finally, we apply the theory to the pyrochlore ruthenates, with particular emphasis on Nd$_2$Ru$_2$O$_7$, and show that it lies in close proximity to the excitonic quantum critical point. Our results establish a microscopic framework for understanding excitonic magnetism in pyrochlore ruthenates and their magnetic excitation spectrum, providing direct connections to spectroscopic probes, including Raman scattering.
summary: This work develops a microscopic theory for excitonic magnetism in ruthenium pyrochlores by analyzing the effective interactions within the low-energy singlet-triplet manifold. It shows that strong spin-orbit coupling can lead to an instability of the nonmagnetic ground state, causing condensation of magnetic excitations (triplons). The resulting phase diagram provides a unified framework connecting theory predictions to experimental measurements in ruthenates.
main_problem: The paper addresses the contradiction between strong spin-orbit coupling suggesting a nonmagnetic singlet ground state in Ru pyrochlores, while experimental evidence shows robust magnetic order.
main_result: The theory predicts that the nonmagnetic singlet state becomes unstable toward triplon condensation as hopping parameters increase, leading to magnetically ordered phases and identifying an additional phase unique to this excitonic description.
method: A microscopic theory is developed using a multi-orbital Hubbard model, deriving effective superexchange interactions within the low-energy singlet--triplet manifold. The analysis employs both spectrum calculations (triplon excitations) and variational treatments of the condensed phase.
model_or_system: The system studied is Ruthenium pyrochlores ($	ext{A}_2	ext{Ru}_2	ext{O}_7$), focusing on $	ext{Ru}^{4+}$ ($d^4$) ions. The model starts from a Hubbard Hamiltonian incorporating SOC and crystal field effects, projecting onto the low-energy singlet--triplet subspace.
key_observables: Triplon gap ($\Delta_{	ext{triplon}}$), magnetization ($\mu_B$), and the magnetic phase diagram as a function of hopping parameters.
important_parameters: Microscopic hopping parameters ($|t_{	ext{o}}/\lambda|$), which govern the transition between non-magnetic and magnetic states.
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on the $t_{2g}$ manifold, and in some sections, a harmonic approximation is used by expanding around the singlet-condensed state.
figures_summary: Figure 1(b) plots the triplon gap and magnetization versus $|t_{	ext{o}}/\lambda|$, showing the transition point. Other figures illustrate the dispersion of triplon bands and lattice structure details.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the single-ion Hamiltonian (including SOC and crystal field), deriving the effective low-energy superexchange Hamiltonian, analyzing the stability via triplon excitation spectra, mapping out the phase diagram, and finally applying the theory to specific ruthenates like $	ext{Nd}_2	ext{Ru}_2	ext{O}_7$.
why_interesting: The concept of excitonic magnetism—where magnetic order arises from bosonic condensation (triplons) rather than localized moments—provides a powerful theoretical lens for understanding correlated materials, linking electronic structure calculations directly to measurable spectroscopic excitations like Raman scattering.
